messages:
olivia: quick QA — after the terraform change to move TLS passthrough to the NLB we're seeing sporadic 502s on the inference gateway. traffic is fine, but healthchecks failing intermittently. anybody seen this pattern?
mike: can you paste the Service + TF snippet? my first guess is targetPort/nodePort mismatch or externalTrafficPolicy change. :thinking_face:
olivia: here's the k8s svc (shortened):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: inference-gateway
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "nlb"
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-preserve-client-ip: "true"
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: inference-gateway
  ports:
  - name: https
    port: 443
    targetPort: 8443
    nodePort: 32043
  externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
```
and the TF that creates target group / lb attachment: 
```hcl
resource "aws_lb_target_group" "inference" {
  name     = "inference-tg"
  port     = 443
  protocol = "TCP"
  target_type = "ip"
  health_check {
    enabled = true
    protocol = "TCP"
    port = "traffic-port"
    interval = 30
  }
}
```
we recently tried switching health-check to TCP to avoid running TLS on health probe. 502s started after that.
ben: a couple quick notes: NLB healthchecks for target_type=ip will call the pod IPs directly on the port you give. since externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster, kube proxy will SNAT, so the nodePort path might be different. often healthchecks hit an endpoint that doesn't respond to plain TCP if the container expects TLS handshake. are you terminating TLS in the pod on 8443?

olivia: yes pod expects TLS on 8443 (certs mounted via k8s secret). the idea was NLB passthrough so no termination in LB.
mike: two things to try: 
1) set externalTrafficPolicy: Local so healthchecks hit the node where pod is and preserve client IP — required if you want nodePort style healthchecks to reach the pod ip path reliably.
2) or change target_group to use target_type = "instance" and point healthcheck at nodePort instead of pod ip — but that changes scaling/behaviour and we usually avoid instance targets for multi-AZ infra.

jia: also check the Gateway/Secret binding: if SNI is used and the NLB is TLS passthrough the LB doesn't terminate TLS so the LB-level healthcheck can't use HTTPS. TCP is fine but the container must accept raw TCP probes (i.e., no ALPN expecting TLS handshake). If your app expects a TLS handshake, a TCP healthcheck that just opens socket should still succeed, but some apps drop before accept if they expect client hello. do our pod containers accept early TCP connects?

olivia: they do accept at accept(2) and then TLS handshake. TCP open should be enough. But we see healthcheck connection reset after ~5-10s sometimes which triggers tg to mark unhealthy.
sre-bot: reminder: NLB cross-zone + target_type = ip + health_check: traffic-port can surface weird ephemeral port mapping depending on kube-proxy. Confirm kube-proxy mode (iptables vs ipvs) and NodePort allocation.

ben: another angle — are we using PROXY protocol? if the app doesn't understand proxied connections it might close. for NLB we usually enable proxy-protocol only for TCP and configure ingress to accept it. check service annotation `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-proxy-protocol` or the gateway config if using Gateway API.

olivia: we did enable proxy protocol earlier for another svc but not this one. annotation not present here. doesnt look like proxied headers are the issue.
mike: i'd try the simplest change first: set externalTrafficPolicy: Local and redeploy svc. That will make node health probes hit the nodePort on the node (and then kube-proxy will forward to pod without SNAT). If you still see 502s, switch health_check port to explicit nodePort (32043) in the TG to avoid any target-port resolution confusion.

jia: small config note: when target_type=ip and you point TG at port 443, the NLB will dial the pod IP:443. But your service uses targetPort 8443 — how is kube routing figuring that out? Usually with type=NodePort the LB targets nodes, not pod IPs, unless we're using externalTrafficPolicy=Local + annotation for target_type ip. There's subtle interactions. Could be that TG->podIP:443 is used but pod listens on 8443 so mismatch -> 502. double-check the resolved port.

olivia: aha — that's suspicious. I assumed TG port 443 would be mapped to service port 443 -> targetPort 8443 by kube-proxy, but maybe with target_type=ip the LB bypasses node proxy. So TG is hitting podIP:443 and not 8443. That'd explain resets.

mike: exactly. two fixes: set TG port to 8443 or change service so port and targetPort match 443. we usually keep targetPort equal to port to avoid confusion when using ip targets.

olivia: ok i'll try changing svc.targetPort to 443 (move container to listen on 443) is annoying. instead i'll change the TG to port = 8443 and health_check port = "traffic-port" so it's consistent. will do a canary in prod AZ1.

ben: +1. also add a quick infra comment in TF: why TG uses 8443 — so next person doesn't revert.
olivia: did the canary, TG updated to 8443, healthchecks stabilized in AZ1. rolling to other AZs now. so root cause: TG->podIP:443 mismatch to container 8443 when using target_type=ip. thanks all. :tada:
deploy-bot: deploy history: aws_lb_target_group.inference updated 1 -> 2 at 2025-10-12T14:10:02Z
mike: nice catch. follow-up: we should add a unit test or lint rule in TF module to prevent TG port != svc.targetPort for ip targets. filing infra ticket.
olivia: filing infra ticket now and adding note to PR. thanks everyone! :heart:
